extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of humor research, linguistics, and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of major theories of verbal humor (SSTH, GTVH, OSTH) and identification of mechanisms that a satisfactory theory should account for.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSTH: 'two scripts' / script opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is characterized by the same text fitting two incompatible 'scripts' (a linguistic construct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical example: patient/lover in the doctor-wife joke (J1). The author argues that applying this formula often requires coercion and misses important mechanisms; the mere existence of two opposing possibilities (A vs. non-A) is not sufficient to explain funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH: Knowledge Resources (KR) framework
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH augments SSTH by adding multiple 'Knowledge Resources' (e.g., target, logical mechanisms, situation, narrative strategy, language) to complement script opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper critiques GTVH for lack of order or coherence (becoming hazy and multi-faceted) and questions how some KRs (e.g., 'target') function as explanatory resources rather than labels. A useful theory should explain how KRs connect and produce humor, not merely enumerate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSTH: ontological semantic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: OSTH (Ontological Semantic Theory of Humor) claims to relate joke meanings to meanings in reality and links to Ontological Semantic Technology for NLP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes boastful claims (e.g., 'no exceptions') and warns against theories that assert universality without robust explanatory evidence or annotated examples. Theories should avoid unfalsifiable absolute claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and specificity of theoretical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory theory should be coherent (internally consistent) and specific enough to be meaningfully critiqued or applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrow, coherent theories are attackable and informative; overly broad or nebulous frameworks become impossible to evaluate. Avoid making the theory so vague that any counterexample is dismissed by rhetorical defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsifiability / openness to counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory should allow and engage with counterexamples rather than claiming 'no exceptions' or acting as the sole authorized critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author criticizes 'proof by intimidation' tactics and urges theories to accept criticism and be empirically testable; do not respond to counterexamples by asserting exclusive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: essentialism vs non-essentialism
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory's scope should indicate whether it aims to be essentialist (one mechanism for all humor types) or fragmentary (different theories for different types).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author views fragmentation ('non-essentialism') as a drawback if it severs verbal humor from non-verbal humor. A good theory should either justify its limited domain or provide connections across types (derision, slapstick, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting 'joke is only a linguistic entity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume jokes are solely linguistic entities; words are not the only carriers of meaning—events, situations, and actions carry meanings too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues many jokes hinge on meanings of actions and situations (intentions, drives) and that a linguistic-only approach misses these. Theories should incorporate non-linguistic carriers of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of thoroughly annotated examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories should support claims with detailed, annotated joke analyses rather than terse labels or unsubstantiated 'fits all jokes' declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes scarcity of thoroughly annotated jokes among proponents; good practice is to provide step-by-step analyses showing how mechanisms operate in examples, avoiding coercive reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding coercion: minimal forced-fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should not 'coerce' jokes to fit the theoretical mold; minimal coercion indicates a more natural explanatory fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many attempts to force jokes into 'two scripts' require unnatural reinterpretations. A criterion for theory adequacy is how naturally examples map onto the proposed mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for implicitness and the role of implicit inference
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis must attend to implicitness — inference required by the listener and the role of unstated assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicitness often enhances funniness (e.g., (J4) doctor's implicit aggression). Theories should explain how implicit inference contributes to humor and why less obvious changes of interpretation often increase funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'eye of the beholder' — perception shift mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can arise from a shift where attention moves from the observed object to the observer's perception (perception over reality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Twain quote (J5), coffee without cream (J6), and 'who wanted the clean cup?' (J3). Theories should model shifts from external facts to the perceiver's mental representation as a source of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detachment of intentions / 'Man plans, God laughs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often derives from detachment of planning and intentions from outcomes—voiding of intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prisoner on way to gallows (J8), green bananas (J2), slipping on a banana peel; the theory must explain how severing identification with intentions produces comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loading with meaning (meaning-loading mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedic mechanism where an initially innocuous element (name, phrase, situation) is 'loaded' with a new, more interesting meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Darling' chauffeur joke (J11), Stupid/Nobody/Nothing (J12), bishop/vicar note (J13). Theories should explain not just a generic 'switch of meanings' but why certain loaded meanings are salient and humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detachment of drives / loss of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor may result when actions are emptied of their motivating drives or passions, rendering them mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: brothel 'patience' (J16), old couple sexual nostalgia (J17), 'I don't remember why' (J18). Theories should capture the move from motivated action to mechanical action as comedic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype-based humor and mechanical behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory must account for jokes based on stereotypes, where behavior conforms to a trait (mechanical) rather than two competing conceptual scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues SSTH struggles here; Bergson's 'mechanical behavior' (trait puppet) better explains stereotype jokes (e.g., stingy Scots). The theory should explain why expected trait-based exaggeration is funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration / hyperbole with declaration-then-illustration structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbolic jokes typically declare an extreme trait and then illustrate it; the exaggeration detaches concept from reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Your mama is so fat...' (J22), 'Joe is so miserly...' (J21). Theory should explain why declaration followed by impossible illustration produces detachment and humor, not merely 'possible vs impossible.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and presentation order (information before/after punchline)
rubrics_metrics.description: The order in which inferred information is presented affects whether a joke succeeds; presenting inferred information before the punch line can make it misfire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in discussion of (J4): if implicit inferences are presented before punchline, funniness is reduced. Theories should model temporal sequencing of information in joke comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit aggression / targeting as explanatory element
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jokes derive funniness from implicit aggression or a target of derision; theory should identify how 'targeting' contributes to humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GTVH lists 'target' as a KR, but the author criticizes treating it as mere label. Useful analysis explains how aggression/targeting interacts with other mechanisms (e.g., detachment, loading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common denominator: detachment of meaning from its carrier
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed unifying mechanism: in many humorous mechanisms, meaning detaches from its carrier (words, actions, situations), allowing carriers to take on new meanings or remain unattached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author summarizes how eye-of-beholder, loading with meaning, detachment of drives, and exaggeration all instantiate detachment. A compelling theory should incorporate this higher-level principle as explanatory glue.
